context: The Prāsaṅgika destination: phenomena exist only as nominal designations. Search behind the label → MI RNYED PA → STONG PA NYID. What remains is MING TZAM — avoiding CHAD LTAR while negating inherent existence.

meaning: object of negation; that which is to be refuted; the negandum
notes: DGAG = negation + BYA = gerundive nominalizer. Sanskrit: pratiṣedhya.
context: The pivotal challenge of the view. Too broad = CHAD LTAR; too narrow = SGRO 'DOGS. The DGAG BYA (inherent existence) was never there — not removed but recognized as always absent. Something that is not there.

notes: THOGS = obstruction + BCAS = having/with. Opposite: THOGS MED.
context: Material phenomena (THOGS BCAS) vs. immaterial (THOGS MED = mind, space, emptiness). Maps onto GZUGS / GZUGS MED.

translit: NAM MKHA' YANG NI MING TZAM
meaning: even space is merely a name; space too is nothing but a label
notes: NAM MKHA' = space/sky; YANG NI = even/also (emphatic)
context: Space — the strongest candidate for independent existence as an unconditioned phenomenon — is also MING TZAM. Closes every escape route for inherent existence.

meaning: where could there be such a view? how could such a view exist?
notes: LTA = view; GA LA = rhetorical "where/how?" (emphatic negative); YOD = exists
context: Even the view of emptiness cannot be grasped as inherently existing. Nāgārjuna: clinging to emptiness itself is the subtlest SGRO 'DOGS.

meaning: name-bearer; that which has a name; the named/referent
notes: MING = name + CAN = possessing/having
context: MING and MING CAN are mutually dependent (RTEN 'BREL) — neither established independently. The referent behind the label is MI RNYED PA; yet conventionally both function — MING TZAM without CHAD LTAR.

meaning: harmed/invalidated by reasoning; contradicted by rational analysis
notes: RIGS PA = reasoning/logic + GNOD = to harm/invalidate
context: One of four criteria for identifying provisional (DRANG DON) meaning. In Madhyamaka: inherent existence is RIGS PAS GNOD — collapses under analysis → MI RNYED PA → MING TZAM.

meaning: "Not a drop" (lit. "wherein is there fault? — there is none")
notes: NYES PA = fault/transgression. MA = negative. Poetic/verse usage.
context: Proclamation of primordial purity (KA DAG): from the ultimate perspective not even a drop of inherent fault exists. The DGAG BYA was never there. Requires GDENG BROD — not mere intellectual assertion.

meaning: confidence, certainty, assurance; trust in one's realization
notes: From GDENG BA = to be confident, to have assurance
context: The inner certainty arising from genuine realization — self-validating, unshakeable, antidote to THE TSOM (doubt). A teacher transmits GDENG as well as information.

meaning: to proclaim with confidence; to roar one's realization
notes: GDENG = confidence + BROD = to proclaim/roar forth
context: GDENG is the inner certainty; GDENG BROD is that certainty given full voice — the lion's roar (SENG GE'I NGA RO). GANG LA NYES PA MA proclaimed as GDENG BROD: realization thrown out without reservation.

notes: GZHI = basis + GRUB = proven/established. Emphasis on epistemic provability.
context: Synonymous with CHOS, SHES BYA, YOD PA, and YUL — all coextensive. GZHI GRUB foregrounds epistemic status: it can be established through valid cognition and brought forward as a legitimate subject of inquiry. The subject of debate must be GZHI GRUB before analysis begins.

meaning: thing, existing thing, a teaching, reality, the truth, duty
notes: Sanskrit: dharma. From root dhṛ = to hold, to sustain. CHOS = whatever holds its own nature (RANG GI NGO BO 'DZIN PA).
context: One of the most semantically rich words in Tibetan — simultaneously phenomenon (anything that exists), Dharma (the Buddha's teaching), and right conduct. Synonymous with SHES BYA, GZHI GRUB, YOD PA, YUL. CHOS foregrounds ontological status: it holds its own nature. The teachings (CHOS) are teachings about phenomena (CHOS) — the ambiguity is a feature, not a bug.

notes: SHES = to know + BYA = gerundive nominalizer. Sanskrit: jñeya.
context: Synonymous with CHOS, GZHI GRUB, YOD PA, YUL. SHES BYA foregrounds cognitive accessibility: it falls within the scope of a knowing mind. In Dharmakīrti's epistemology, defined by causal efficacy — if something can perform a function it can be known, and vice versa. There is no gap between existence and knowability.

notes: Sanskrit: deṣa (place/region) and viṣaya (object/domain). Covers both spatial and cognitive senses.
context: Synonymous with CHOS, SHES BYA, GZHI GRUB, YOD PA. YUL foregrounds the relational aspect: not just that something exists and can be known, but that it stands as the object of a particular cognitive act. YUL CAN = subject (literally "that which has an object"). The YUL/YUL CAN structure is itself an expression of GNYIS SNANG (dualistic appearance).

notes: YOD = to exist, there is + PA (nominalizer). Opposite: MED PA (non-existent, absence).
context: The most basic member of the synonymy cluster — the bare existential affirmation. If something is YOD PA it is automatically CHOS, SHES BYA, GZHI GRUB, and YUL. In Madhyamaka the crucial question is not whether something is YOD PA but *how* — inherently (RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS) or merely nominally (MING TZAM). YOD PA by itself is neutral; the qualifier is everything.

notes: GZHAN = other + LUGS = system/position/tradition + DGAG PA = to refute/negate. LUGS carries the sense of a whole philosophical system, not just a single claim.
context: One of the two classic movements of Buddhist philosophical writing — paired with RANG LUGS SGRUB PA (establishing one's own position). Central to the Prāsaṅgika method: Nāgārjuna and Candrakīrti operate almost exclusively through DGAG PA, driving opponents toward unwanted consequences (THAL 'GYUR) rather than asserting positive theses. Whether Prāsaṅgikas have a RANG LUGS at all is itself one of the great debates in the tradition.

meaning: (skt: nitya) unchanging, unchanging thing, permanent, eternal
notes: Sanskrit: nitya. RTAG = constant/permanent + PA (nominalizer). Defined as a phenomenon that is NOT momentary (SKAD CIG MA MIN PA). Opposite of MI RTAG PA.
context: In Buddhist epistemology 'permanent' does not mean everlasting or truly existent — it means non-momentary, not changing instant to instant. RTAG PA covers unconditioned phenomena: uncompounded space (NAM MKHA'), cessations, and above all negations/absences (DGAG PA). These are static: they do not arise, abide, and disintegrate. Contrast with DNGOS PO, which by definition performs a function and therefore must change. A key early distinction in the Collected Topics (BSDUS GRWA).

notes: Sanskrit: anitya. MI (negation) + RTAG PA. Defined as that which is momentary (SKAD CIG MA) — produced and disintegrating in each instant.
context: Coextensive with DNGOS PO (functioning thing), BYAS PA (product), and 'DUS BYAS (compounded phenomenon): whatever is impermanent is a functioning thing, and vice versa. The 'impermanence' at stake is subtle — not merely that things eventually break down, but that they disintegrate moment by moment, never enduring into a second instant. This momentariness is the engine of Dharmakīrti's system: only what changes can perform a function, and only what performs a function is real.

meaning: (skt: bhava) working thing, functioning thing, thing
notes: Sanskrit: bhāva. Defined as DON BYED NUS PA — 'that which is able to perform a function.' Coextensive with impermanent thing (MI RTAG PA) and product (BYAS PA).
context: The cornerstone of Dharmakīrti's ontology: to be real (DNGOS PO) is to be causally efficacious. Anything that can produce an effect is a functioning thing; anything that cannot (like space or a negation) is RTAG PA and, in the strict sense, not a 'thing' at all. This is why DNGOS PO is often translated simply 'thing' — for the pramāṇa tradition, the causally potent particular is what genuinely exists. Its opposite, DNGOS MED, means non-functioning phenomenon (a permanent phenomenon), not sheer non-existence.

notes: The reason-marking particle. Follows the stated reason (RTAGS / GTAN TSHIGS) in a formal statement. Fuller form: ...YIN PA'I PHYIR ('because it is...').
context: The syntactic backbone of Tibetan logical debate. A formal proof runs [subject] [predicate] YIN TE, [reason] YIN PA'I PHYIR — 'It is the case that (subject) is (predicate), because (reason).' PHYIR closes the reason clause the way 'because' does in English, but always sits at the END of it, since Tibetan is head-final. Recognizing PHYIR is the fastest way to locate the reason in any argument you are reading.

notes: Past/perfective sense: 'established, proven, accomplished.' Sanskrit: siddha. Appears in GZHI GRUB (provable/existing thing) and GRUB PA (that which is established).
context: To say something is GRUB is to say it is established as existing by valid cognition (TSHAD MA) — it holds up under analysis and can be brought forward as a legitimate object of debate. This is the same GRUB as in GZHI GRUB from the foundation session. It also carries the yogic sense of 'accomplished' (as in DNGOS GRUB, siddhi — spiritual attainment), but in a debate context it almost always means 'proven / established as existent.'

meaning: suppose someone says... (lit: if one mouth said...)
notes: Literally 'if one mouth said...': KHA = mouth + CIG = a certain/one + NA RE = quotative particle introducing reported speech. Idiomatically 'a certain someone says.'
context: The standard debate-manual formula for introducing an opponent's position (PHYOGS SNGA MA, Sanskrit pūrvapakṣa) before refuting it. A passage typically runs KHA CIG NA RE ... ZER ('some say ... they claim'), after which the author dismantles the view. Spotting KHA CIG NA RE tells you immediately that what follows is a position the author intends to knock down, not their own view — essential for reading philosophical texts without being misled.

notes: KHYAB PA = pervasion (Sanskrit: vyāpti), the relation of logical entailment. 'A KHYAB B' = wherever A holds, B necessarily holds. Negated as MA KHYAB ('does not necessarily follow').
context: The heart of Buddhist logic. A correct reason must satisfy pervasion: if something is the reason, it must necessarily be the predicate (e.g. 'whatever is produced is necessarily impermanent'). In live debate the defender answers a challenge with 'DOD (I accept), RTAGS MA GRUB (the reason is not established), or MA KHYAB (there is no pervasion — your reason doesn't entail your conclusion). KHYAB is thus one of the three or four words on which the entire dialectic turns.

notes: Quotative verb marking an asserted claim, frequently an opponent's. Commonly closes the phrase opened by KHA CIG NA RE.
context: Where KHA CIG NA RE opens a reported position, ZER typically closes it: '...ZER' = '...they claim.' Because it flags an assertion attributed to someone, ZER often signals a view about to be examined or refuted, in contrast to the author's own voice. Distinguished from neutral 'to say' by this argumentative coloring — in a debate text, 'X ZER' usually means 'the opponent claims X.'

meaning: the subject of a debate, the thing which has a quality, "let's consider this topic"
notes: Sanskrit: dharmin. CHOS = quality/property/phenomenon + CAN = 'possessing' (the suffix meaning 'that which has'). So 'the property-possessor' — the subject about which something is predicated.
context: The technical term for the SUBJECT of a syllogism or debate — the thing whose properties are under discussion. In 'sound is impermanent because it is produced,' sound is the CHOS CAN. It is appended directly after the subject to flag it: SGRA CHOS CAN — 'sound, the subject...' — effectively 'take sound as our topic.' Note the pairing with CHOS from the foundation session: CHOS is the quality, CAN marks its possessor. The CHOS CAN must itself be GZHI GRUB (an established, existing basis) before any analysis of it can begin.

notes: The distal demonstrative — 'that,' pointing to something farther off or already mentioned. Contrasts with 'DI ('this'). Also serves as the third-person pronoun 'it / that one.'
context: One of the workhorses of Tibetan prose and debate. Combined with particles it builds key connectives: DE PHYIR / DE'I PHYIR = 'therefore,' DE LTAR = 'thus / in that way,' DE DAG = 'those (plural),' DE NYID = 'that very thing / suchness.' Because Tibetan has no definite article, DE frequently does the work of 'the' — re-pointing to a subject already established as the CHOS CAN.

notes: The proximal demonstrative — 'this,' pointing to something near or immediately at hand. The near/far pair with DE ('that'). Written with the a-chung ('A) prefix.
context: Used to introduce or point directly at the matter under discussion — often the subject just raised for analysis. Builds parallel connectives to DE: 'DI LTAR = 'in this way / as follows' (frequently introducing an explanation), 'DIR = 'here / in this case.' Where DE re-points to something already in play, 'DI foregrounds what is present now.

notes: Sanskrit: prasaṅga. THAL = to follow (as a consequence) + 'GYUR = to become / turn into. Together: a consequence that follows from an opponent's own position.
context: The signature move of Madhyamaka dialectic and the namesake of the Prāsaṅgika school (THAL 'GYUR PA). Rather than asserting a positive thesis, Candrakīrti and Nāgārjuna drive the opponent to an unwanted consequence entailed by their own claims (e.g. 'then it would absurdly follow that...'). In live debate THAL marks the consequence hurled at the defender, who must answer 'DOD (accept), RTAGS MA GRUB (reason unestablished), or MA KHYAB (no pervasion). Closely tied to KHYAB and PHYIR from the earlier sessions.

notes: Sanskrit: buddha. A two-part translation: SANGS = awakened / purified (cleared away, as from sleep) + RGYAS = expanded / fully blossomed. Not a phonetic rendering but an interpretive one.
context: The Tibetan coinage deliberately unpacks buddhahood into two movements the single Sanskrit word only implies: SANGS, the purification and clearing away of every obscuration and fault, and RGYAS, the full flowering and expansion of every excellent quality and realization. A buddha is thus one in whom all that must be removed has been removed and all that can be developed has been perfected — the twofold sense the translators built directly into the word.

meaning: Arya, realized being, a person who has seen emptiness directly
notes: Sanskrit: ārya. Literally 'the exalted / superior one.' 'PHAGS = to be raised up, exalted + PA (nominalizer). Marks a being who has risen above the ordinary state.
context: Technically, an 'PHAGS PA is one who has directly and non-conceptually perceived emptiness (STONG PA NYID) — reaching the path of seeing (MTHONG LAM) and beyond. This direct realization is what 'exalts' them above the SO SO SKYE BO (ordinary being), who at best understands emptiness only inferentially. The term spans all four Buddhist vehicles (arya-śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas are all 'PHAGS PA) and appears in 'PHAGS PA'I BDEN PA BZHI, the Four Noble ('Arya') Truths — truths as seen by the realized.

meaning: Accept, Assert, Agree, Is, Say, Desire
notes: Sanskrit: iṣṭa (accepted / desired). A high-frequency verb spanning two clusters of sense: (1) to accept / assert / hold as one's position, and (2) to want / desire. Context decides which.
context: In debate, 'DOD is the defender's single most important word: the reply ''DOD' — 'I accept' — concedes the consequence (THAL 'GYUR) just thrown at them, as opposed to challenging the reason (RTAGS MA GRUB) or the pervasion (MA KHYAB). More broadly it marks any asserted position ('so-and-so 'DOD' = 'so-and-so holds that...'). Its other life is 'to desire': the same root gives 'DOD CHAGS (desire-attachment), one of the root afflictions. Reading it correctly means catching whether the passage is about a claim being held or an object being wanted.

notes: Sanskrit: iṣṭa. The defender's answer conceding the point. Also carries the broader senses 'accept, assert, hold, is, say, desire' (see the 05 Ben's Text entry). Here it is specifically the debate response of assent.
context: One of the three core replies available to a defender facing a stated reason or consequence (THAL 'GYUR). Answering 'DOD accepts the claim as it stands — as opposed to the two rejections: RTAGS MA GRUB (the reason doesn't apply) and KHYAB PA MA BYUNG (the entailment fails). Choosing among these three is the fundamental rhythm of the debate courtyard.

meaning: Why?, Why would you say that?
notes: ACIP kept as written in class ('CI SPHYIR'); the standard spelling is CI'I PHYIR — CI = what + 'I (genitive) + PHYIR = because/for the sake of → 'for what reason?' The Tibetan shown (ཅིའི་ཕྱིར) is the standard form. A close variant is CI PHYIR.
context: The challenger's demand for a reason. When a thesis is put forward, the questioner asks 'why?' — forcing the defender to supply the reason (RTAGS / GTAN TSHIGS) that will then itself be tested for whether it is established (GRUB) and whether it pervades (KHYAB). It is the pivot that turns a bare assertion into a full statement of reason.

meaning: reason is not establish (never say this), 1 isn't 3 (mostly don't say this), Sound is not made (in the context of sound is a changing thing because it's made.)
notes: RTAGS = reason/sign + MA (negation) + GRUB = established. The three clauses are escalating registers of the same answer: the blunt literal form (avoid), a softer 'it doesn't apply here' form, and the contextual form for the stock example 'sound is a changing thing because it's made.'
context: One of the two ways to reject a stated reason. RTAGS MA GRUB denies that the reason actually applies to the subject (CHOS CAN) — the sign itself is not established in this case. Contrast with KHYAB PA MA BYUNG, which grants that the reason applies but denies that it entails the conclusion. In 'sound is a changing thing because it's made,' this rejection targets the reason's applicability (claiming sound isn't made), not the logical link.

meaning: the necessity doesn't arise (never say this!), there is no necessary relationship (mostly don't say this), Just because something is made doesn't mean it has to be changing (in the context of sound is a changing thing because it's made.)
notes: KHYAB PA = pervasion/entailment + MA (negation) + BYUNG = arose/occurred. The three clauses are escalating registers: the blunt literal form (avoid), a softer 'no necessary relationship' form, and the contextual form for the stock example. Equivalent to the common courtyard answer MA KHYAB.
context: The second way to reject a stated reason — the counterpart to RTAGS MA GRUB. Here the defender grants that the reason applies but denies the pervasion (KHYAB): the reason does not necessarily entail the conclusion. In 'sound is a changing thing because it's made,' this reply grants that sound is made but denies that being made forces being changing. Together, 'DOD, RTAGS MA GRUB, and KHYAB PA MA BYUNG are the complete set of a defender's answers, each targeting a different part of the argument.

notes: Case 1 (Nominative): the subject of a verb. Case 8 (Vocative): direct address. No particle is added — the noun stands alone.

translit: SU RU TU DU NA RA LA
notes: Case 2 (Accusative/Direct Object — ex: at, to): the object of an action. Case 4 (Dative/Beneficial — ex: for): the recipient or beneficiary. Case 7 (Locative — ex: at, on, in): location or direction. Choice of particle determined by the final letter of the preceding syllable.

script: གྱིས་ གིས་ ཀྱིས་ འིས་ ས་ ཡིས་
notes: Case 3 (Agentive/Instrumental — ex: by, with): marks the agent of a transitive verb or the instrument by which an action is performed. Choice of particle determined by the final letter of the preceding syllable.

Case 6 (Genitive/Possessive/Connective — ex: 's, of): marks possession, connection, or modification between nouns. One of the most frequent particles in Tibetan. Choice of particle determined by the final letter of the preceding syllable.

Case 5 (Ablative/Originative — ex: from, than, then): marks the source, origin, or point of departure of an action. Also used for comparison (than) and temporal sequence (then, after). NAS tends toward source/sequence; LAS toward origin/comparison.

meaning: Says in scripture, honorific for says
notes: The honorific past of GSUNG BA, 'to speak' — used only for exalted speakers: the Buddha, lamas, and the scriptures themselves. Ordinary speech uses ZER or SMRA instead. GSUNG is also the honorific noun 'speech,' as in SKU GSUNG THUGS (enlightened body, speech, and mind).
context: The standard marker of scriptural citation: ZHES GSUNGS ('thus it is said') closes a quotation and flags it as the word of an authority. In philosophical texts this signals an appeal to scripture (LUNG) as opposed to reasoning (RIGS PA) — the two accepted sources of proof. Tibetan verbs shift by register of respect, and GSUNGS is the clearest example the class has met: the same act of saying, but elevated because of who says it.

notes: Sanskrit: ākāśa. NAM = sky/heavens + MKHA' = space. The final a-chung (') is part of the spelling: MKHA', not MKHA.
context: The stock example of an unchanging thing (RTAG PA) in debate. Space is defined negatively — the mere absence of obstructing contact — so it exists but performs no function, making it the classic instance of a DNGOS MED (non-thing) to set against DNGOS PO like a water pitcher. Whenever a debate needs 'something permanent,' space is the first example reached for. The Extended deck's NAM MKHA' YANG NI MING TZAM ('even space is merely a name') uses it the same way: if even space is a mere label, everything is.

meaning: So then...., meaning if you accept A you must accept this!
notes: The verb that ends a statement of consequence — 'it follows that...' Root of THAL 'GYUR (implication, consequence — see 05 Ben's Text) and of the school name THAL 'GYUR PA (Prāsaṅgika, 'the consequence school').
context: In the courtyard this single syllable is the hammer of the challenger's move. The full pattern runs: [subject] CHOS CAN, [predicate] THAL, [reason] PHYIR — 'take the subject; it follows that it is X; because it is Y' — delivered with the hand-clap. Everything the defender then says ('DOD, RTAGS MA GRUB, or KHYAB PA MA BYUNG — see 06 Debate Foundations) is a response to what THAL just asserted: that their own position forces this conclusion on them.

notes: GZHAN = other + YANG = also/again — literally 'also otherwise,' i.e. 'beyond that.' Ben wrote it with the ACIP comma, which is the shad (།) — the particle typically ends its clause. GZHAN on its own is the ordinary word for 'other' (compare GZHAN DBANG, 'other-powered,' in the Extended deck).
context: A discourse connective that stacks a further argument onto one already made. Philosophical texts chain refutations with it: a first absurdity is driven home, then GZHAN YANG — 'moreover...' — and another one begins. It joins the toolkit of structural signposts from 05 Ben's Text (DE PHYIR 'therefore,' DE LTAR 'thus'): words that don't carry doctrine themselves but tell you where you are in the argument.

meaning: can, to be able, potential, possibility, capacity, ability
notes: The verb 'to be able' and the stem of NUS PA, 'ability, power, potency.' Follows another verb to mean 'can': BYED NUS = 'can do.'
context: The hinge of the thing/non-thing divide. A working thing (DNGOS PO — see 04 Ben's Text) is defined as DON BYED NUS PA, 'that which is able to perform a function' — so NUS is literally the word the definition turns on. What can produce an effect is a thing; what cannot (like space) is DNGOS MED. The noun NUS PA also names the potency or capacity carried in a cause — the power of a seed to sprout — making this small verb load-bearing across both logic and the theory of causation.

notes: Sanskrit: abhāva. DNGOS (PO) = working thing + MED = does not exist / is without → 'without thingness.' The direct negation of DNGOS PO (see 04 Ben's Text).
context: The other half of the fundamental division of existents: everything that exists is either a working thing (DNGOS PO) or a non-thing (DNGOS MED). A DNGOS MED exists — it can be known and debated about — but performs no function and produces no effects: unchanging phenomena like space (NAM MKHA') and mere absences. The stock debate form puts the pieces of this session together: 'the subject, space, is a non-thing, because it cannot perform a function' — NAM MKHA' CHOS CAN, DNGOS MED YIN PAR THAL, DON BYED MI NUS PA'I PHYIR.

meaning: real individual instance of a generality, a thing that exists by definition or through it's own definitive qualities
notes: Sanskrit: svalakṣaṇa. RANG = own/self + MTSAN (NYID) = defining characteristic. Short for RANG GI MTSAN NYID KYIS GRUB PA — 'a thing which exists through its own definition or definitive qualities.'
context: In the epistemology (TSHAD MA) tradition the class is entering, RANG MTSAN are the real particulars — the actual functioning things out in the world, grasped nakedly by direct perception. This water pitcher, this fire: each exists through its own defining character rather than through a label. The pair to hold together is RANG MTSAN vs SPYI MTSAN: the individual instance versus the general category it instantiates. The divide maps onto this session's other pair — RANG MTSAN line up with working things (DNGOS PO), SPYI MTSAN with non-things (DNGOS MED).

meaning: A general thing, in the sense of being an idea, catagory, or archetype
notes: Sanskrit: sāmānyalakṣaṇa. SPYI = general / universal + MTSAN = characteristic. The counterpart of RANG MTSAN.
context: What conceptual thought actually works with: not the individual fire in front of you (a RANG MTSAN) but 'fire' the category — an idea, archetype, or mental image standing in for all its instances. A SPYI MTSAN exists, but only as an abstraction: it is unchanging and performs no function, placing it on the DNGOS MED side of the divide. This is the tradition's account of why thought and perception differ — perception meets the particular directly, while thinking always goes through the general image.

notes: The plural particle. Follows the noun it pluralizes: SANGS RGYAS RNAMS = 'buddhas,' CHOS RNAMS = 'phenomena.'
context: Tibetan nouns are number-neutral — SANGS RGYAS can mean one buddha or many — so plurality is left unmarked unless it matters, and RNAMS is the standard way to mark it. It is everywhere in scripture and verse ('CHOS RNAMS THAMS CAD...' — 'all phenomena...'). The other common pluralizer is DAG, met inside DE DAG ('those') in the 05 Ben's Text notes; RNAMS is the more frequent and more neutral of the two.
